title: History, Quarantine, and When to Optimize
purpose: Make the three recurring silver-layer decisions explicit: whether the table needs SCD Type 2 history or a plain overwrite, what happens to records that fail a quality rule, and when to spend a physical rewrite on OPTIMIZE and V-Order.
accessibleSummary: A decision tree with three questions. The first asks whether anyone needs to see the state of a row as it was at a past point in time: if yes, the table needs SCD Type 2 history; if no, an overwrite or snapshot is simpler and cheaper. The second asks what should happen to records that fail a quality rule — quarantine them and keep the good records flowing, or fail the whole batch when partial data would be worse than none. The third asks whether the table is read-heavy enough to justify V-Order and compaction, which is disabled by default in new Fabric workspaces and costs roughly fifteen percent more write time. A warning branch covers the specific failure of resolving the latest row without a deterministic ordering key.
longDescription: This is a decision tree covering the three questions that recur on almost every silver table. Question one is about history: SCD Type 2 is justified only when someone genuinely needs to reconstruct the state of a row as of a past date; otherwise an overwrite or snapshot is simpler, cheaper, and easier to reason about. Question two is about failure handling: quarantine keeps good records flowing and isolates the bad ones for correction and replay, but it is only honest if a replay path actually exists; failing the batch outright is the right call when partial data downstream would be worse than no data. Question three is about physical layout: V-Order improves downstream read performance across Fabric engines and pays off most in read-heavy dashboarding and repeated scans, but Microsoft states it costs roughly fifteen percent longer on writes, and it is disabled by default in new workspaces. Because toggling the table property only affects future writes, applying it to existing data requires a physical rewrite via OPTIMIZE. The warning node captures the classic silver bug: resolving the latest row per key without a deterministic ordering column, which corrupts history non-reproducibly on every retry.

nodes.label: Does anyone need the row as it was?
nodes.summary: The history question: SCD Type 2 is justified by a real point-in-time requirement, nothing less.
nodes.detail: Ask whether any consumer genuinely needs to reconstruct a row's state as of a past date — a price as it stood at time of sale, an address as it was when the contract was signed. If nobody does, SCD Type 2 is complexity without a customer.
nodes.whyItMatters: SCD Type 2 changes the grain of the table, the shape of every downstream join, and the cost of every query against it. Adopting it speculatively imposes that cost permanently on a requirement that may never arrive.

inputs: The consumer questions the table must answer
Whether any of them are 'as of' questions
Regulatory or reconciliation requirements for point-in-time reconstruction
processing: List the questions asked of this entity
Mark which ones require a past state rather than the current state
If none do, stop — the table does not need Type 2
outputs: A yes or no that routes to Type 2 history or to overwrite/snapshot
drill.example: A product dimension is asked only 'what is this product called now', never 'what was it called when that order shipped' — so it is overwritten, not versioned.
controls: Require a named 'as of' question before adopting Type 2
failureModes: Applying Type 2 to every dimension by convention and paying the join cost forever
Discovering the history requirement after the fact, with no way to reconstruct what was overwritten

nodes.label: SCD Type 2 history
nodes.summary: Version the row: close the old record, open a new one, keep both.
nodes.detail: Under SCD Type 2, a change closes the current version of the row and opens a new one, so the table holds every state the entity has ever been in with validity ranges. This requires a deterministic ordering key so changes are applied in the order they truly happened — which is precisely where the warning node applies.
nodes.whyItMatters: It is the only structure that answers 'as of' questions correctly. It is also the structure most often implemented with a subtly non-deterministic ordering, which corrupts history quietly.

inputs: Change records with a business key
A deterministic ordering column — source commit time or a monotonic sequence
The set of attributes whose change should trigger a new version
processing: Order changes deterministically by the ordering key, never by arrival order
Close the current row by setting its validity end, and insert the new version
Merge idempotently, so a replayed batch does not create duplicate versions
outputs: A versioned Delta table with validity ranges per row
The ability to reconstruct any entity's state as of any past date
drill.example: A customer's address change is applied by source commit time; the previous row's validity is closed and a new row opened, so an order from last year still joins to the address that was current then.
controls: A deterministic ordering key, enforced and tested
An idempotent merge key so retries are safe
failureModes: Applying changes in arrival order rather than event order, producing a plausible but wrong history
A non-idempotent merge that duplicates versions when a batch is replayed

nodes.label: Overwrite or snapshot
nodes.summary: No point-in-time requirement, so keep the current state and skip the versioning cost.
nodes.detail: Where only the current state is ever asked for, overwrite the row or take a periodic full snapshot. Delta still supplies ACID guarantees and time travel over the underlying Parquet files, so a limited amount of history remains recoverable without modelling it explicitly.
nodes.whyItMatters: It keeps the table at its natural grain and its joins simple. Delta's time travel means choosing this does not leave you with literally no recourse if a past state is needed for recovery.

evidence.note: All managed lakehouse tables use Delta, which supplies ACID transactions, schema enforcement, and time travel over the underlying Parquet files.

inputs: A business key to match on
processing: Merge on the business key, updating in place
Or write a periodic full snapshot where the source has no reliable change signal
outputs: A current-state table at its natural grain
Delta time travel available for recovery, though not modelled as business history
drill.example: A product reference table is merged on product key each night; only the current name and category are kept, and Delta time travel covers accidental-overwrite recovery.
controls: Do not lean on Delta time travel as if it were business history — retention is bounded
failureModes: Treating time travel as an SCD Type 2 substitute and discovering the retention window has passed

nodes.label: What happens to records that fail a rule?
nodes.summary: Second question: quarantine the bad records, or fail the whole batch?
nodes.detail: When a record violates a quality rule, there are two honest options. Quarantine isolates the bad records and lets the good ones proceed — but only if a replay path genuinely exists. Failing the batch stops everything, which is correct when partial data downstream would be worse than no data at all.
nodes.whyItMatters: Choosing quarantine without building the replay path is the worst of both worlds: bad records vanish into a table nobody reads, and the data silently becomes incomplete without anyone being alerted.

inputs: The quality rules and their severities
Whether downstream consumers can tolerate partial data
Whether anyone will actually own and work the quarantine table
processing: Classify each rule: does violating it invalidate the record, or the whole batch?
For quarantine, commit to a replay path and an owner before enabling it
For fail-fast, make the alert loud enough that someone acts on it
outputs: An explicit, owned failure policy per rule rather than an implicit one
drill.example: A missing optional attribute quarantines the single record; a source file with the wrong schema fails the whole batch, because loading half a day's orders would be worse than loading none.
controls: Every quarantine table has a named owner and a replay procedure
Reconciliation counts published per run: loaded, quarantined, rejected
failureModes: A quarantine table that grows forever because nobody owns it — silent, permanent data loss
Failing the batch on a trivial rule and blocking a day's data for a cosmetic violation

nodes.label: Is this table read-heavy enough for V-Order?
nodes.summary: Third question: V-Order costs ~15% on writes and is off by default — spend it where reads dominate.
nodes.detail: V-Order is a write-time optimisation that improves downstream read performance across Fabric engines, and it pays off most in read-heavy patterns such as dashboarding, interactive analytics, and repeated scans. Microsoft states the tradeoff as writes taking roughly 15% longer on average. It is disabled by default in newly created Fabric workspaces — a deliberate default favouring write-heavy ingestion pipelines.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is a genuine tradeoff with a published cost, not a free win. Enabling it on a write-heavy staging table pays the write penalty for read acceleration nobody uses.

evidence.note: V-Order is a write-time Parquet optimisation improving downstream read performance across Fabric engines; it pays off most in read-heavy patterns like dashboarding, interactive analytics, and repeated scans.
Microsoft states the typical tradeoff as writes taking roughly 15% longer on average, in exchange for reads that can improve significantly depending on workload.
V-Order is disabled by default in newly created Fabric workspaces, a deliberate default favouring write-heavy ingestion and transformation pipelines.

inputs: Whether the table backs dashboards or repeated interactive scans
The current V-Order setting, which defaults to off in new workspaces
processing: Classify the table as read-heavy (dashboards, repeated scans) or write-heavy (staging, transient)
Enable V-Order only on the read-heavy ones
Remember that toggling the table property affects only future writes — existing files keep their layout
outputs: V-Order applied where reads dominate, and left off where writes do
A conscious ~15% write cost accepted only where it buys read performance
drill.example: A gold table backing an executive dashboard has V-Order enabled and is compacted; the bronze staging table it is built from is left at the workspace default of off.
controls: Control V-Order at the session config, the Delta table property, or the per-write option — noting session and write settings take precedence over the table property
failureModes: Enabling V-Order globally and paying ~15% on every write, including write-heavy staging tables that are scanned once
Expecting a property change to reformat existing data — it does not

nodes.label: OPTIMIZE to rewrite existing files
nodes.summary: Toggling the property only affects future writes — existing data needs a physical rewrite.
nodes.detail: Because toggling the V-Order table property only affects future writes, files already on disk keep the layout they were written with. Applying or removing V-Order across existing data therefore requires a physical rewrite via table compaction — OPTIMIZE. This is also the step that consolidates the small files that incremental merges accumulate.
nodes.whyItMatters: Teams routinely enable the property, see no improvement, and conclude V-Order does not work. It does — but only for data written after the change, unless OPTIMIZE rewrites what is already there.

evidence.note: Toggling the V-Order table property only affects future writes; files already on disk keep their layout, so applying or removing V-Order on existing data requires a physical rewrite via compaction (OPTIMIZE).

inputs: A table whose V-Order setting has just changed
A table accumulating small files from incremental merges
A maintenance window with capacity headroom
processing: Run OPTIMIZE to compact small files and physically rewrite them in the new layout
Schedule it against the table's actual write cadence, not on a fixed arbitrary timer
outputs: Compacted Delta files carrying the intended V-Order layout
Fewer, larger files for downstream scans to read
drill.example: After enabling V-Order on a gold table, OPTIMIZE is run once to rewrite the existing files; without it, only rows written from that point forward would have been accelerated.
controls: Run OPTIMIZE after any V-Order property change, or the change is a no-op for existing data
Budget the capacity the rewrite consumes
failureModes: Enabling the property, skipping OPTIMIZE, and concluding V-Order delivers nothing
Running OPTIMIZE so frequently that the rewrite cost exceeds the read benefit

nodes.label: Trap: 'latest row' with no ordering key
nodes.summary: Resolving the latest row per key without a deterministic ordering column corrupts history — differently each retry.
nodes.detail: The classic silver bug: deduplicating to the 'latest' row per business key using arrival order, file order, or an unstable timestamp. It usually looks correct, because most of the time the orders coincide. On a retry, a late-arriving file, or a reshuffled partition, it silently picks a different winner — and an SCD Type 2 table built on it records a history that never happened.
nodes.whyItMatters: The failure is non-deterministic, so it does not reproduce on demand and it does not fail loudly. It just quietly writes a different history each time the job runs.

inputs: Change records with more than one row per business key in a batch
The column currently being used to decide which one wins
processing: Identify a genuinely deterministic ordering key — source commit time, a monotonic sequence, or an LSN
Break ties explicitly, so two rows with the same timestamp still resolve identically every run
Make the merge idempotent so a replay reproduces the same result exactly
outputs: Deduplication that produces the same winner on every run
An SCD Type 2 history that is reproducible rather than incidental
drill.example: Two updates for one customer land in the same batch with identical processing timestamps; without a tiebreak, the winner depends on partition order, so the recorded address differs between two runs of the same input.
controls: A deterministic ordering key plus an explicit tiebreak, tested with a deliberately reordered replay
failureModes: Using ingestion or file-arrival time as if it were event time
Assuming a same-second tie will not happen, so leaving the tiebreak undefined

edges.label: no — only the current state matters
read-heavy — and existing files need rewriting

walkthrough.title: 1. Does anyone ask 'as of'?
walkthrough.explanation: SCD Type 2 needs a real point-in-time requirement. Without one, it is permanent complexity with no customer.

walkthrough.title: 2. If yes, version the row
walkthrough.explanation: Close the old version, open the new one — and order the changes deterministically.

walkthrough.title: 3. If no, overwrite
walkthrough.explanation: Keep the natural grain. Delta time travel still covers accidental-overwrite recovery.

walkthrough.title: 4. Quarantine, or fail the batch?
walkthrough.explanation: Quarantine only if a replay path and an owner genuinely exist; otherwise it is silent data loss.

walkthrough.title: 5. Spend V-Order where reads dominate
walkthrough.explanation: It is off by default and costs roughly 15% on writes — enable it on read-heavy tables, not staging.

walkthrough.title: 6. OPTIMIZE to rewrite what already exists
walkthrough.explanation: The property only affects future writes; existing files keep their layout until compaction rewrites them.

walkthrough.title: 7. Avoid the non-deterministic latest row
walkthrough.explanation: Without a deterministic ordering key, each retry can record a different history — and none of them fail loudly.
